analysis.one_liner: Charges fossil fuel companies for the carbon in their fuels and sends the money to every American in equal quarterly dividends.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with no cosponsors and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it died without a hearing or vote when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require companies that produce or import oil, coal, and natural gas to buy permits each year for the carbon their fuels will release, with the number of permits shrinking from 15% below 2015 emissions in 2025 to 90% below by 2050. All the auction money would go into a trust fund and be paid out in equal quarterly dividends to every lawfully present American with a Social Security number. It would also tax carbon-heavy imports and rebate exporters, add air-quality monitoring in communities near pollution sources, and shield climate-related lawsuits from being preempted.
analysis.who_benefits: Every lawfully present U.S. resident with a Social Security number would receive an equal quarterly cash dividend funded entirely by fees on oil, coal, and natural gas producers. Because wealthier households tend to burn more fossil fuel, the dividend would act as a modest redistribution from heavy consumers to ordinary households. People living near refineries, mines, and power plants would also benefit from required co-pollutant reductions and new air monitoring.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyday households receiving quarterly climate dividends

how_it_helps.text: Each eligible person would receive an equal, tax-free quarterly dividend out of the auction proceeds, which mostly offsets the higher fuel costs that fall hardest on lower-income households.
The bill caps U.S. carbon emissions on a declining schedule — starting 15% below 2015 levels in 2025 and reaching 90% below by 2050 — with a minimum permit price of $40 per ton rising $10 a year.
It requires pollution reductions in frontline communities to keep pace with overall carbon cuts, and expands air-quality monitoring near those communities.

It imposes border fees on carbon-intensive imports (steel, cement, aluminum, and similar goods) so foreign producers cannot undercut U.S. firms that pay for permits, and refunds those costs on U.S. exports.

analysis.who_pays: Producers, importers, and sellers of coal, oil, and natural gas would pay for permits at a rising minimum price ($40 per ton, increasing $10 a year plus inflation), with penalties of triple the permit price for noncompliance. Energy-intensive manufacturers would face higher fuel costs, cushioned by border fees on imports and export rebates. Consumers would initially pay some of these costs in fuel and utility prices until dividends arrive.

drawbacks.text: Fossil fuel companies would pass the cost of permits to consumers in the prices of gasoline, electricity, and heating, so households would face higher energy costs before receiving their first dividend.

The bill mandates steep cuts — 50% below 2015 emissions by 2030 and 90% by 2050 — which could strain regions and workers dependent on coal, oil, and gas industries, and it contains no dedicated transition aid for those workers or communities.
Dividends would only go to lawfully present individuals with valid Social Security numbers, excluding some residents who would still pay the higher fuel prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — steady per-person dividends plus steep emissions cuts — is real and the design is defensible: auctions rather than free giveaways, anti-hoarding limits, and border fees to prevent industry flight. The drawbacks are serious: fossil-fuel price increases would reach consumers through electricity, gasoline, and heating before dividends arrived, and the pace of cuts (50% by 2030) would be among the fastest ever attempted. The bill, however, was never seriously considered — introduced in the final weeks of a Congress with no cosponsors and no committee action — so no legislative weighing of these tradeoffs actually occurred.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in mid-December 2024 and sat there with no hearing, no vote, and no cosponsors until the Congress ended three weeks later.

narrative.text: Sen. Van Hollen introduced the bill on December 11, 2024, in the final weeks of the 118th Congress.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day, where no further action was taken.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, without the bill ever receiving a hearing or a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers and major carbon emitters avoided paying for their emissions, and no carbon-pricing system was created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers avoided carbon costs

for.name: Sen. Chris Van Hollen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in December 2024 and got it referred to the Finance Committee.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no action — no hearing, markup, or vote — before the Congress ended.

against.name: Fossil fuel and electric utility industry groups
against.what_they_did: Have historically opposed carbon-pricing legislation that charges fuel producers for emissions.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred; the bill attracted zero cosponsors from either party, so no support pattern was ever recorded.

industries.industry: Coal, oil, and natural gas producers
industries.note: They would buy permits for every ton of carbon in the fuels they sell, at a rising minimum price, under a cap shrinking to 90% below 2015 levels by 2050 — the direct target of the bill.
Higher fuel and energy costs would hit them, though border fees on comparable imports and export rebates would offset much of the competitive loss.

industries.industry: Clean energy and air-quality monitoring sectors
industries.note: A shrinking carbon allowance and rising permit floor price would push demand toward non-fossil energy, and the bill funds expanded pollution monitoring.
